--------
In this VladTV interview, Denvonta “Dirt Rocc” Lee breaks down how Las Vegas authorities tracked him down and subpoenaed him to testify in Keefe D’s murder trial tied to the 1996 killing of Tupac Shakur. Speaking with Vlad, he recalls being approached at a gas station, weighing whether to refuse, and realizing investigators could still force him into court. Dirt Rocc describes the pressure of taking the stand for the first time and says much of what surfaced had already been discussed publicly.

The conversation also revisits Reggie Wright Jr., Reggie Wright Sr., Mob James, Eddie Amin of the Outlawz, Orlando Anderson, Southside Crips history, and how VladTV interviews were played in court. Vlad and Dirt Rocc discuss Keefe D’s book, his public statements, Las Vegas detectives, alleged Puffy connections, and why Keefe’s own words may have made him the most important witness in the case.

--------
Ramon “Mundo” Mendoza sits down with Vlad to recount life after his 1975 release, describing why the streets of Los Angeles felt more violent than prison. He details reconnecting with Joe Morgan, Sailor Boy, and Mexican Mafia associates while attempting to organize heroin distribution through local dealers, with ties mentioned to Glendale, Folsom, the Aryan Brotherhood, and Crystal Maria Alonzo of the Manson circle. Mendoza also reflects on the dangers faced by patrol officers in cities like LA, New York, and Philadelphia, where armed criminals may be heading to or leaving crime scenes.

In a chilling account, Mendoza says Alfie Salsa moved from getaway driver to designated shooter after demanding a bigger role, ultimately becoming one of the Mexican Mafia’s most prolific street killers, with “over 20” alleged hits. A raw true crime discussion on organized crime, prison gangs, and the underworld before modern cartel-era violence.

In this VladTV conversation, combat veterans Nicholas Irving and Robert O’Neill react to Vlad’s update on the Lil Durk murder-for-hire case, including the Beverly Hills shooting, federal evidence, co-defendants, cell phone tracking and the rapper’s not-guilty outcome as described in the interview. The discussion broadens into how surveillance, vehicles, phones and digital habits shape modern investigations in Los Angeles and beyond. Irving references the DC sniper attacks in Washington, D.C., Maryland and Virginia, while O’Neill draws on military experience to explain why electronic footprints have exposed targets overseas. The two also talk tactics in pop culture, from Heat and Val Kilmer’s reload scene to SAS training influences, Call of Duty, Nintendo and the rise of drone operators. The interview closes with reflections from Afghanistan, the war on terror, PTSD, extremism and how upbringing can fuel violence.

--------
TS Madison sits down with Vlad for a candid conversation about childhood identity, growing up trans, and the pressures young people face around gender and sexuality. Madison reacts strongly to Boosie’s comments about allowing teenage sons and nephews to have sexual experiences with adult women, arguing that adults normalizing that behavior can create lasting emotional damage and unhealthy views of intimacy.

The discussion also explores Madison’s early experiences being labeled “different,” family pressure around masculinity, and how society often grooms children into rigid gender roles while accusing LGBTQ people of doing the same. Vlad and TS Madison also debate youth transitioning, hormones, and the example of Jazz Jennings, with Madison reflecting on starting her own transition as a teenager and the complicated feelings that come with it.

They close by addressing homophobia, transphobia, religion, the Bible, acceptance, and what it means to live authentically.
